questions.stem: A nurse is found to have practiced significantly outside their legal scope of practice, as defined by their state's Nurse Practice Act, after performing a procedure well beyond their training. Potential consequences the nurse should understand may include:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fairly few consequences beyond a simple verbal warning, without much regard for the seriousness of the scope-of-practice violation","B":"Fairly little meaningful consequence at all, since Nurse Practice Acts are mistakenly assumed here to function just as informal guidelines","C":"Disciplinary action by the state board of nursing, which may include license suspension or revocation, given the seriousness of this scope-of-practice violation","D":"Automatic criminal prosecution occurring with no involvement from the state board of nursing in this kind of scope-of-practice case"}}
questions.rationale: Violating a state's Nurse Practice Act can result in disciplinary action by the state board of nursing, ranging from a reprimand to license suspension or revocation, depending on the severity of the violation, since the Nurse Practice Act carries the force of law, not merely guideline status.
questions.source_name: NCSBN — Nurse Practice Act Enforcement and Disciplinary Actions
questions.source_detail: Consequences of Scope of Practice Violations

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to renew their nursing license. Many states require which component as part of this process?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Completion of an entirely new nursing degree program is required before license renewal is even possible","B":"No specific renewal requirements exist in any U.S. state for a licensed nurse seeking to renew","C":"Retaking the full NCLEX licensure examination again at the time of every routine license renewal cycle","D":"Completion of a specified number of continuing education hours, in addition to other state-specific requirements"}}
questions.rationale: Many states require nurses to complete a specified number of continuing education hours (along with other requirements, which vary by state) as part of the license renewal process, supporting ongoing professional competency and knowledge updates.
questions.source_name: NCSBN — State Licensure Renewal Requirements
questions.source_detail: Continuing Education for License Renewal

questions.stem: A nursing peer review process is used at a facility to evaluate a nurse's clinical practice after an adverse event involving a medication error, and the nurse worries this process exists solely to end their career. This process is best described as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A formal evaluation process used just for physicians, with fairly little equivalent review process actually available for nurses","B":"A structured, professional evaluation process, often conducted by colleagues, meant to assess practice and find areas for improvement","C":"A process that deliberately bypasses due process for the nurse being formally reviewed by their own nursing colleagues","D":"A purely punitive process with termination of employment as its sole intended outcome, offering fairly little real path to improvement"}}
questions.rationale: Nursing peer review is a structured, professional evaluation process, often conducted by nursing colleagues, used to assess clinical practice, particularly following adverse events, with the goal of quality improvement and professional development, generally following defined due process procedures, rather than being purely punitive.
questions.source_name: ANA — Peer Review Guidelines for Nursing Practice
questions.source_detail: Purpose and Structure of Nursing Peer Review

questions.stem: A charge nurse is determining the appropriate staff mix (RN, LPN, UAP) for a unit's upcoming shift that includes several newly admitted, high-acuity clients. This decision should be based primarily on:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A random staffing assignment made with fairly little specific criteria applied regarding the unit's actual current client acuity","B":"A single, fixed staffing ratio that never changes regardless of the unit's client acuity levels, including these new high-acuity admissions","C":"The acuity and care needs of the client population, including these new high-acuity admissions, along with the scope of practice and competency of each staff type","D":"Staff seniority alone, applied with fairly little consideration of the unit's actual current client care needs or new admissions"}}
questions.rationale: Determining an appropriate staff mix should be based on the acuity and specific care needs of the client population on the unit, matched against the scope of practice, skills, and competency of RNs, LPNs, and unlicensed assistive personnel, to ensure safe, appropriate care delivery.
questions.source_name: ANA — Principles for Nurse Staffing, Staff Mix Considerations
questions.source_detail: Basis for Determining Appropriate Staff Mix

questions.stem: A nurse is completing documentation in a client's medical record after a challenging shift, and a colleague suggests it's fine to be vague since "no one really reads these anyway." The nurse understands that this documentation actually serves as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A largely optional record that carries fairly little formal legal significance if it were ever formally reviewed by anyone involved","B":"A document that can be freely altered after the fact with fairly little formal notation of the change actually required","C":"A record whose relevance is limited just to billing and reimbursement purposes, with fairly little legal weight if it were ever reviewed","D":"A legal record of care that can be used in legal proceedings and should be accurate, timely, and complete"}}
questions.rationale: Medical record documentation serves as a legal record of the care provided and can be used as evidence in legal proceedings. It should be accurate, timely, complete, and objective, and any corrections should follow proper protocol (such as a single line through an error with initials, date, and time) rather than being altered or deleted.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Legal Aspects of Documentation
questions.source_detail: Documentation as a Legal Record

questions.stem: A nurse catches a medication error before it reaches the client (a "near miss") and reports the event through the facility's reporting system, though a colleague questions why they bothered since no harm actually occurred. This reporting is important because:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Near-miss events offering fairly little meaningful value for ongoing patient safety improvement efforts across the whole organization","B":"Just events that result in actual, confirmed client harm should ever be formally reported to leadership at any point","C":"Analyzing near misses helps identify system vulnerabilities before they cause actual harm, supporting proactive safety improvement","D":"Reporting a near-miss event being treated as largely optional and rarely encouraged by most facilities in a situation like this one"}}
questions.rationale: Reporting and analyzing near misses (errors caught before reaching the client) is a valuable, proactive patient safety practice, since it helps identify system vulnerabilities and contributing factors before they result in actual patient harm, allowing for preventive improvements.
questions.source_name: AHRQ / IHI — Near Miss Reporting and Patient Safety Culture
questions.source_detail: Value of Near Miss Reporting

questions.stem: A care team faces a complex ethical dilemma regarding a client's treatment plan, with the family wanting aggressive treatment continued and several team members believing it is now causing more suffering than benefit. An appropriate resource in this kind of disagreement is to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Making a unilateral treatment decision on behalf of the team, with fairly little further consultation sought from an outside resource","B":"Request a consultation with the facility's ethics committee, which can provide a structured process to help address this kind of disagreement between the family and team","C":"Involving just the facility's legal counsel, largely bypassing any ethical discussion of the underlying disagreement between the parties","D":"Deliberately avoiding the underlying ethical concern altogether, hoping the disagreement between the family and team resolves on its own eventually"}}
questions.rationale: Ethics committees provide a structured, multidisciplinary process to help address complex ethical dilemmas in patient care, offering consultation, education, and policy guidance when there is disagreement or uncertainty about the ethically appropriate course of action.
questions.source_name: ASBH (American Society for Bioethics and Humanities) — Healthcare Ethics Consultation Standards
questions.source_detail: Role of the Ethics Committee

questions.stem: A nurse educator explains the difference between "cultural competence" and "cultural humility" to a new graduate who assumes that completing a single cultural training module means they've now mastered the topic. Cultural humility instead emphasizes:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"That cultural considerations are largely irrelevant to the delivery of nursing care in a modern healthcare setting, contrary to what the educator is actually teaching","B":"Completion of a single training session, with no further ongoing self-reflection required afterward, similar to what the new graduate is currently assuming","C":"Achieving a fixed, complete mastery of every possible cultural background and belief system that exists, similar to what the new graduate is assuming","D":"An ongoing process of self-reflection, learning, and recognizing power imbalances, rather than the one-time mastery the new graduate is currently assuming"}}
questions.rationale: Cultural humility emphasizes an ongoing, lifelong process of self-reflection, critical self-awareness, and recognition of power imbalances in the patient-provider relationship, in contrast to "cultural competence," which can imply achieving a fixed, complete mastery of cultural knowledge — an idea increasingly viewed as unattainable given the diversity within any cultural group.
questions.source_name: Transcultural Nursing Society — Cultural Humility Framework
questions.source_detail: Distinguishing Cultural Humility from Cultural Competence

questions.stem: A nurse is comparing general clinical features of hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism. The nurse understands that hyperthyroidism is more typically associated with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Bradycardia and constipation exclusively, findings more typical of hypothyroidism","B":"Weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance, and increased appetite","C":"No significant metabolic changes associated with either thyroid condition","D":"Weight gain, fatigue, and cold intolerance, findings more typical of hypothyroidism"}}
questions.rationale: Hyperthyroidism (excess thyroid hormone) generally increases metabolic rate, presenting with weight loss despite increased appetite, tachycardia, heat intolerance, and often anxiety or tremor — in contrast to hypothyroidism, which typically presents with weight gain, fatigue, cold intolerance, and bradycardia.
questions.source_name: American Thyroid Association — Hyperthyroidism vs. Hypothyroidism Clinical Features
questions.source_detail: General Comparison of Thyroid Dysfunction Presentations

questions.stem: A client with Cushing's syndrome (excess cortisol) is being examined by a nurse who is trying to distinguish this condition from Addison's disease based on physical appearance alone. Which finding would this client with Cushing's syndrome most likely present with?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Significant weight loss accompanied by notable skin hyperpigmentation, findings actually more typical of Addison's disease rather than Cushing's syndrome","B":"Low blood pressure as the primary and most defining clinical feature, a finding more typical of Addison's disease instead","C":"Hypoglycemia as a primary and defining feature, a finding more typical of Addison's disease rather than Cushing's syndrome","D":"A rounded \"moon face,\" central obesity, and a \"buffalo hump\" (dorsocervical fat pad), classic findings that would help the nurse distinguish this from Addison's disease"}}
questions.rationale: Cushing's syndrome, resulting from excess cortisol, classically presents with a rounded "moon face," central (truncal) obesity, a "buffalo hump" (fat deposition at the base of the neck/upper back), thin extremities, purple striae, and often hypertension and hyperglycemia — a distinct pattern from adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease).
questions.source_name: Endocrine Society — Cushing's Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline
questions.source_detail: Classic Physical Findings of Cushing's Syndrome

questions.stem: A nurse is comparing SIADH and diabetes insipidus in terms of fluid and sodium balance. The nurse understands that SIADH is characterized by:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Excessive dilute urine output accompanied by an elevated serum sodium level in this particular case","B":"Excess antidiuretic hormone leading to water retention, dilutional hyponatremia, and concentrated urine","C":"A complete absence of circulating antidiuretic hormone in the bloodstream","D":"No meaningful effect at all on the client's fluid or sodium balance despite the underlying hormonal abnormality"}}
questions.rationale: SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone) involves excess ADH secretion, causing the kidneys to retain water, leading to dilutional hyponatremia and concentrated urine — essentially the opposite pattern of diabetes insipidus, which involves ADH deficiency or resistance, causing excessive dilute urine output and risk of hypernatremia/dehydration.
questions.source_name: Clinical Endocrinology References — SIADH vs. Diabetes Insipidus
questions.source_detail: Pathophysiologic Distinction Between the Two Conditions

questions.stem: A client recovering from acute pancreatitis develops a palpable abdominal mass and persistent abdominal pain several weeks later, and the family assumes this just means the pancreatitis is taking longer than usual to fully resolve. The nurse should suspect this may instead indicate:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A normal, expected finding during recovery that requires no further evaluation, contrary to what this new mass and persistent pain actually suggest","B":"A pancreatic pseudocyst, a recognized complication of pancreatitis requiring further evaluation, rather than simply a slower resolution as the family assumes","C":"An unrelated musculoskeletal finding requiring no further workup, despite the pancreatitis history and location of this new finding","D":"Complete resolution of the client's pancreatitis with no ongoing concern, contrary to what this new mass and pain actually suggest"}}
questions.rationale: A pancreatic pseudocyst is a recognized complication that can develop weeks after an episode of acute pancreatitis, presenting with a palpable abdominal mass, persistent pain, or other symptoms, and requires further evaluation (such as imaging) to confirm and guide management.
questions.source_name: American College of Gastroenterology — Acute Pancreatitis Complications
questions.source_detail: Pancreatic Pseudocyst as a Delayed Complication

questions.stem: A client with advanced liver cirrhosis is being evaluated, and a family member asks whether cirrhosis really affects anything beyond the liver itself. The nurse should explain that this client is at risk for which serious complications related to portal hypertension, addressing the family's question?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Just skin-related complications, with fairly little involvement of the gastrointestinal system","B":"Esophageal varices (risk of life-threatening bleeding) and ascites (fluid accumulation in the abdomen), both complications extending well beyond the liver itself","C":"Fairly little meaningful relationship between cirrhosis and other body systems beyond the liver itself","D":"An improvement in overall liver function with no associated risk of complication, contrary to the risks this client with advanced cirrhosis actually faces"}}
questions.rationale: Portal hypertension resulting from advanced cirrhosis can lead to serious complications, including esophageal varices (dilated veins at risk of life-threatening rupture and bleeding) and ascites (fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity), both of which require close monitoring and specific management strategies.
questions.source_name: AASLD (American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases) — Cirrhosis Complications Guideline
questions.source_detail: Portal Hypertension Complications: Varices and Ascites

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client with rectal bleeding, and a colleague assumes that because the blood is bright red, the source must definitely be somewhere very low in the GI tract with no other possibility. Bright red blood per rectum (hematochezia) is generally more suggestive of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A lower GI bleed, though a very brisk upper GI bleed can occasionally present similarly, meaning the colleague's assumption isn't entirely certain","B":"A finding with no established relationship to the actual anatomic location of bleeding, contrary to what this finding actually suggests clinically","C":"A normal finding in a client with rectal bleeding, requiring no further evaluation, despite the concerning nature of this symptom","D":"An upper GI bleed exclusively, with no possibility of a lower GI source, which is the opposite of what this presentation actually suggests"}}
questions.rationale: Bright red blood per rectum (hematochezia) is generally more suggestive of a lower GI bleed (such as from the colon or rectum), while dark, tarry stools (melena) are more typical of an upper GI bleed. However, a very brisk upper GI bleed can sometimes present with bright red rectal bleeding due to rapid transit time, so clinical correlation is needed.
questions.source_name: ACG Clinical Guideline — GI Bleeding Localization
questions.source_detail: Hematochezia vs. Melena as Localizing Clues

questions.stem: A client with multiple sclerosis reports new-onset visual disturbances, worsening fatigue, and new numbness that started over the past two days, and asks the nurse if this is just a normal part of daily life with MS that doesn't need attention. The nurse should recognize these findings as consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A normal, entirely unrelated finding with no connection to the client's MS diagnosis, contrary to what these new symptoms actually suggest","B":"Complete remission of the client's underlying multiple sclerosis disease process, contrary to the new symptoms being described","C":"A sign that the client's multiple sclerosis has permanently and fully resolved, contrary to the new symptoms being described","D":"A possible MS exacerbation (relapse), warranting prompt provider evaluation rather than being dismissed as routine, as the client is currently assuming"}}
questions.rationale: New or worsening neurological symptoms in a client with multiple sclerosis, such as visual disturbances, fatigue, or increased numbness, can indicate an MS exacerbation (relapse), warranting prompt evaluation by the provider to confirm and guide appropriate management, such as corticosteroid therapy in some cases.
questions.source_name: National MS Society — Recognizing MS Relapses
questions.source_detail: Signs of MS Exacerbation

questions.stem: A client develops progressive, ascending muscle weakness beginning in the legs, following a recent respiratory illness. The nurse should recognize this pattern as potentially consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Multiple sclerosis exclusively, a diagnosis inconsistent with this rapid, ascending pattern","B":"A normal, self-limited condition requiring no further nursing monitoring","C":"A simple muscle strain unrelated to any recent infectious illness or the client's ascending weakness pattern","D":"Guillain-Barré syndrome, requiring close monitoring for progression to respiratory involvement"}}
questions.rationale: Guillain-Barré syndrome classically presents with progressive, ascending muscle weakness (often beginning in the legs and moving upward), frequently following a preceding infection. Close monitoring for respiratory muscle involvement is critical, since respiratory failure is a serious potential complication requiring prompt intervention.
questions.source_name: GBS/CIDP Foundation International — Guillain-Barré Syndrome Clinical Presentation
questions.source_detail: Ascending Paralysis Pattern and Respiratory Monitoring

questions.stem: A client on warfarin for atrial fibrillation has an INR of 1.4, and the client mentions feeling reassured since the number seems close to a normal reference range they saw online. The nurse should recognize this value as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Below the typical therapeutic range (generally 2.0-3.0 for atrial fibrillation), indicating inadequate anticoagulation and increased clotting risk, contrary to the client's reassurance","B":"Within the typical therapeutic INR range generally targeted for this specific clinical indication, supporting the client's sense of reassurance here","C":"A dangerously elevated INR value, indicating a significantly increased bleeding risk, which is not actually the concern with this particular result","D":"A laboratory value with fairly little established relationship to the client's ongoing warfarin therapy, contrary to what this INR actually reflects"}}
questions.rationale: The typical therapeutic INR range for atrial fibrillation is generally 2.0-3.0. An INR of 1.4 is below this range, indicating inadequate anticoagulation and an increased risk of thromboembolic events, warranting dose adjustment and provider notification.
questions.source_name: ACC/AHA — Atrial Fibrillation Anticoagulation Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Therapeutic INR Range for Atrial Fibrillation

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a client's reticulocyte count, finding it significantly elevated, in a client recovering from a recent significant blood loss during surgery. This finding generally indicates:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A normal, unremarkable finding carrying fairly little meaningful clinical significance, despite the client's recent significant blood loss","B":"Increased red blood cell production by the bone marrow, often in response to anemia or blood loss, fitting this client's recent surgical history","C":"Decreased overall bone marrow activity and red blood cell production, essentially opposite to what this elevated value actually reflects","D":"Fairly little established relationship to the client's red blood cell production, contrary to what this specific lab value actually measures"}}
questions.rationale: An elevated reticulocyte count indicates increased red blood cell production by the bone marrow, often as a compensatory response to anemia, blood loss, or hemolysis, helping differentiate between causes of anemia (such as production problems vs. increased destruction/loss).
questions.source_name: Clinical Laboratory Reference Standards — Reticulocyte Count Interpretation
questions.source_detail: Elevated Reticulocyte Count as a Marker of Bone Marrow Response

questions.stem: A client with a macrocytic anemia (elevated MCV) is being evaluated for the underlying cause, and the provider orders additional labs before considering an iron supplement the client had been taking on their own. The nurse understands this macrocytic pattern is commonly associated with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Chronic blood loss exclusively, a cause that would more typically produce a microcytic rather than macrocytic pattern","B":"A normal variant requiring no further evaluation, despite the provider's decision to order additional labs for this client","C":"Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, a cause consistent with this macrocytic pattern and distinct from the iron supplement the client has been taking","D":"Iron deficiency, a cause more typically producing small, pale (microcytic) cells rather than the large cells seen in this client"}}
questions.rationale: Macrocytic anemia (characterized by an elevated mean corpuscular volume, MCV) is commonly associated with vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, which impair DNA synthesis in developing red blood cells, resulting in larger-than-normal cells, distinct from the microcytic pattern typically seen with iron deficiency.
questions.source_name: Clinical Hematology References — Macrocytic Anemia Causes
questions.source_detail: B12/Folate Deficiency and Macrocytic Anemia

questions.stem: A client with iron deficiency anemia is having lab results reviewed, and a nursing student assumes the MCV would be elevated since the client feels so fatigued. The nurse clarifies that a client with iron deficiency anemia would typically instead have which laboratory finding pattern?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Elevated MCV, reflecting macrocytic rather than microcytic red blood cells, which is not the pattern actually seen with iron deficiency, contrary to the student's assumption","B":"A normal ferritin level paired with an elevated hemoglobin concentration, which does not match the pattern actually seen with iron deficiency anemia","C":"No meaningful changes in any of the client's red blood cell indices, contrary to what iron deficiency anemia would actually be expected to show","D":"Decreased MCV (microcytic), decreased hemoglobin/hematocrit, and low serum ferritin, the actual expected pattern, correcting the student's assumption"}}
questions.rationale: Iron deficiency anemia is classically characterized by microcytic (decreased MCV) red blood cells, decreased hemoglobin and hematocrit, and low serum ferritin (reflecting depleted iron stores), a pattern distinct from the macrocytic anemia seen with B12/folate deficiency.
questions.source_name: Clinical Hematology References — Iron Deficiency Anemia Laboratory Pattern
questions.source_detail: Microcytic Anemia and Ferritin in Iron Deficiency

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to administer a blood transfusion during a trauma resuscitation where there is no time to wait for a full type and crossmatch, and the blood bank sends O negative units. The nurse understands that a client with blood type O negative is generally considered:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A universal donor, whose red blood cells can generally be given to recipients of any ABO/Rh type in an emergency like this one, explaining why these units were sent","B":"A universal recipient, capable of receiving blood of any ABO or Rh type without risk of a transfusion reaction, which describes AB positive rather than O negative","C":"Compatible only with type AB positive blood, with no other blood type considered compatible, which misdescribes the actual compatibility of O negative blood","D":"Incompatible with every other blood type, including in this kind of emergency transfusion situation, contrary to why O negative was actually sent"}}
questions.rationale: Type O negative red blood cells lack A, B, and Rh(D) antigens, making them generally compatible with recipients of any ABO/Rh blood type, which is why O negative is often referred to as the "universal donor" type for red blood cell transfusions, particularly valuable in emergencies when a client's blood type is unknown.
questions.source_name: AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) — Blood Type Compatibility Guidelines
questions.source_detail: O Negative as Universal Donor Type

questions.stem: A nurse is using red blood cell indices (MCV, MCHC) to help classify a client's anemia. The nurse understands that MCV specifically measures:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The average size (volume) of individual red blood cells","B":"The total number of white blood cells present in the client's circulating blood","C":"The client's overall platelet function and clotting cascade activity","D":"The concentration of hemoglobin contained within each individual red blood cell"}}
questions.rationale: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) measures the average size (volume) of individual red blood cells, helping classify anemia as microcytic (small cells), normocytic (normal size), or macrocytic (large cells), which narrows the differential diagnosis for the underlying cause.
questions.source_name: Clinical Laboratory Reference Standards — Red Blood Cell Indices
questions.source_detail: MCV as a Measure of Red Blood Cell Size

questions.stem: A nurse is transferring a client from the bed to a wheelchair. Which action reflects safe transfer technique?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Rushing through the transfer quickly to save time, regardless of the client's current level of stability","B":"Lifting the client's full body weight using only the nurse's own back muscles, without any assistive equipment","C":"Skipping any assessment of the client's mobility level before beginning the wheelchair transfer","D":"Using proper body mechanics, assistive devices as needed, and adequate staff/equipment based on the client's mobility level"}}
questions.rationale: Safe transfer technique involves using proper body mechanics (bending at the knees, not the back), appropriate assistive devices (gait belt, mechanical lift, or transfer board as needed), and ensuring adequate staff and equipment based on an assessment of the client's specific mobility level and needs.
questions.source_name: ANA — Safe Patient Handling and Mobility Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Principles of Safe Client Transfer

questions.stem: A nurse performs a skin assessment on a newly admitted client. Thorough documentation should include:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Specific findings, including any wounds, bruising, rashes, or areas of concern, with precise location, size, and description","B":"Documenting skin findings only at the time of discharge, never at admission, to save initial assessment time","C":"Documenting the skin only if an abnormality happens to be found during the initial assessment","D":"A brief, general statement of 'skin normal' with no further descriptive detail provided in the chart"}}
questions.rationale: Thorough skin assessment documentation should include specific findings — such as the precise location, size, and description of any wounds, bruising, rashes, or other areas of concern — establishing a clear baseline at admission that supports ongoing monitoring, communication, and potential legal/quality documentation needs.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Skin Assessment Documentation Standards
questions.source_detail: Essential Elements of Skin Assessment Documentation

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the medication list of an older adult client taking twelve different medications prescribed by four separate providers who don't appear to communicate with one another. The nurse should recognize increased risk of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An improvement in overall health outcomes with no additional associated risk from this many medications and prescribers","B":"No established relationship between the total number of medications and this client's overall safety, despite the number of prescribers involved","C":"A decreased need for formal medication reconciliation given how many prescribers are already involved in this client's care","D":"Polypharmacy-related risks, including drug interactions, adverse effects, and medication errors, given the number of medications and uncoordinated prescribers"}}
questions.rationale: Polypharmacy (use of multiple medications, particularly common in older adults with multiple conditions and providers) increases the risk of drug-drug interactions, adverse effects, and medication errors. Regular medication reconciliation and review are important strategies to reduce these risks.
questions.source_name: American Geriatrics Society — Polypharmacy in Older Adults
questions.source_detail: Risks Associated with Polypharmacy

questions.stem: A nurse is providing discharge teaching about home fall prevention for an older adult client. Which recommendation is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Leave loose rugs and clutter in place on the floor, in order to preserve familiarity in this particular case","B":"Remove loose rugs and clutter, ensure adequate lighting, and install grab bars in the bathroom as needed","C":"Encourage the client to walk independently through poorly lit areas of the home","D":"Avoid recommending any home modifications, since they are considered unnecessary"}}
questions.rationale: Evidence-based home fall prevention recommendations for older adults include removing loose rugs and clutter, ensuring adequate lighting throughout the home (especially stairways and bathrooms), and installing grab bars in the bathroom, among other environmental modifications to reduce fall risk.
questions.source_name: CDC — STEADI Initiative, Home Fall Prevention Recommendations
questions.source_detail: Environmental Modifications to Reduce Fall Risk

questions.stem: A nurse is providing health promotion counseling about injury prevention. Which statement reflects an evidence-based recommendation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Seatbelts are thought to increase overall injury risk and should generally be avoided during vehicle travel","B":"Seatbelt use recommendations apply only to children, with no relevance to adult passengers","C":"Seatbelt use is considered optional, since it offers no significant established safety benefit","D":"Consistent seatbelt use significantly reduces the risk of serious injury or death in a motor vehicle collision"}}
questions.rationale: Consistent seatbelt use is a well-established, evidence-based recommendation that significantly reduces the risk of serious injury or death in the event of a motor vehicle collision, a core message in general injury prevention health promotion counseling for all age groups.
questions.source_name: CDC — Motor Vehicle Safety, Seatbelt Use Recommendations
questions.source_detail: Seatbelt Use and Injury Prevention

questions.stem: A nurse is providing sun safety education to parents of young children. Which recommendation is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use sun protection strategies, including sunscreen (for infants over 6 months), protective clothing, and shade, given the cumulative risk of UV exposure starting in childhood","B":"Sun exposure during childhood carries no meaningful long-term health implications for the child later in life","C":"Applying sunscreen only once per day, regardless of swimming or continued outdoor activity afterward","D":"Sunscreen use is considered unnecessary for children under any circumstance, regardless of UV exposure level"}}
questions.rationale: Sun safety education for children includes recommending sun protection strategies such as sunscreen (generally recommended for infants over 6 months, with shade and protective clothing prioritized for younger infants), protective clothing, and seeking shade, since UV exposure in childhood contributes to cumulative lifetime skin cancer risk.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Sun Safety for Children
questions.source_detail: Sun Protection Recommendations for Children

questions.stem: A community health nurse promotes "Mental Health First Aid" training for community members. This training is designed to help participants:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Actively avoid any interaction with an individual experiencing an acute mental health crisis","B":"Fully replace the need for professional mental health treatment in most situations encountered by community members","C":"Recognize signs of mental health or substance use challenges and provide initial support, connecting individuals to appropriate professional help","D":"Independently diagnose a specific mental health condition for a community member based on the training alone"}}
questions.rationale: Mental Health First Aid training is designed to help community members recognize signs and symptoms of mental health or substance use challenges, provide initial support and reassurance, and connect individuals to appropriate professional resources — similar in concept to physical first aid, but for mental health concerns, not intended to replace professional diagnosis or treatment.
questions.source_name: National Council for Mental Wellbeing — Mental Health First Aid Program
questions.source_detail: Purpose and Scope of Mental Health First Aid Training

questions.stem: A client with PTSD experiences a flashback during a nursing assessment, becoming pale and appearing to relive a traumatic event from years earlier while staring blankly past the nurse. The nurse's most appropriate initial action is to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Leave the room immediately, with no attempt at further intervention or support for this visibly distressed client","B":"Ignore the client's visible distress and continue the planned nursing assessment exactly as originally scheduled","C":"Speak calmly, help ground the client in the present moment (e.g., using their name, describing the current safe environment), and provide reassurance","D":"Ask the client detailed questions about the traumatic event while the flashback is actively occurring, in order to gather more history right then"}}
questions.rationale: During a flashback, a trauma-informed approach involves speaking calmly, helping ground the client in the present moment (using orienting cues such as their name, the current date, and safe surroundings), and providing reassurance, rather than pressing for details about the traumatic event during the acute episode.
questions.source_name: National Center for PTSD — Managing Flashbacks and Trauma Responses
questions.source_detail: Grounding Techniques for Flashback Management

questions.stem: A client with a history of heavy alcohol use is hospitalized and, two days later, develops severe tremors, confusion, hallucinations, and autonomic instability. The nurse should recognize this as consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Simple anxiety that requires nothing more than verbal reassurance from the nurse","B":"Delirium tremens (DTs), a life-threatening complication of alcohol withdrawal requiring prompt treatment","C":"A normal, expected withdrawal symptom that requires no urgent nursing action","D":"An unrelated psychiatric condition with no connection to the client's alcohol history in this particular clinical scenario overall"}}
questions.rationale: Delirium tremens is a severe, potentially life-threatening complication of alcohol withdrawal, typically developing 48-96 hours after the last drink, presenting with severe tremors, confusion, hallucinations, and autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, fever). It requires prompt recognition and treatment, often with benzodiazepines, in a monitored setting.
questions.source_name: ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) — Alcohol Withdrawal Management Guideline
questions.source_detail: Recognition of Delirium Tremens

questions.stem: A nurse is providing guidance to a parent about how to support their 5-year-old child after the death of a grandparent, and the parent asks whether they should just explain it the same way they would to an adult relative. The nurse should explain that children's understanding of death:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Being essentially the same as an adult's understanding, without much regard for the particular child's actual age or developmental stage","B":"Meaning young children should be largely shielded from any discussion of the death, contrary to what supporting this grieving child actually requires","C":"Not being considered a relevant factor when providing support to a grieving child of any developmental stage, contrary to what actually guides this support","D":"Varies by developmental stage, meaning support should be tailored to this particular 5-year-old's cognitive and emotional level rather than explained the same way as to an adult"}}
questions.rationale: Children's understanding of death varies significantly by developmental stage (e.g., young children may not grasp the permanence of death, while older children and adolescents have a more mature understanding). Support and communication should be tailored to the child's specific developmental level, using honest, age-appropriate language rather than complete avoidance of the topic.
questions.source_name: National Alliance for Grieving Children — Developmental Understanding of Death
questions.source_detail: Age-Appropriate Grief Support for Children

questions.stem: A parent asks the nurse whether aspirin is safe to give their 10-year-old child, who has a fever from a suspected viral illness. The nurse's best response is:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Aspirin should be avoided in children and teenagers with viral illnesses such as flu or chickenpox, due to the risk of Reye syndrome; acetaminophen or ibuprofen are safer alternatives","B":"Aspirin should be given at double the usual adult dose for faster fever relief in a child with a viral illness","C":"Aspirin carries no known risk at all when given to a child experiencing a viral illness like the flu or chickenpox","D":"Aspirin is considered safe and the preferred medication choice for fever in children of any age group"}}
questions.rationale: The FDA, CDC, and AAP recommend avoiding aspirin in children and teenagers under 19 with viral illnesses (such as flu or chickenpox), due to its association with Reye syndrome, a rare but serious and potentially fatal condition. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen are generally recommended alternatives for fever in this population.
questions.source_name: FDA — Reye Syndrome Warning for Aspirin Products
questions.source_detail: Aspirin Contraindication in Children with Viral Illness

questions.stem: A client presents with a deep, contaminated puncture wound from a rusty fence post and cannot recall their last tetanus vaccination, though they believe it may have been over a decade ago. The nurse should anticipate the provider will likely order:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Tetanus prophylaxis (vaccine, possibly with immune globulin depending on wound type/history), per current guidelines, given this history","B":"Oral antibiotics alone, with fairly little consideration given to the client's uncertain tetanus vaccination status or this wound's type","C":"Fairly little prophylaxis needed at all, without much regard for the client's uncertain vaccination history and this particular wound's contamination","D":"Just wound cleaning performed, without factoring in the client's uncertain tetanus history or how this particular wound occurred"}}
questions.rationale: For contaminated or deep wounds with an uncertain or incomplete vaccination history, tetanus prophylaxis (Td/Tdap vaccine, and tetanus immune globulin for certain wound types) is indicated per standard wound management guidelines, in addition to appropriate wound cleaning and care.
questions.source_name: CDC — Tetanus Wound Management Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Tetanus Prophylaxis Based on Wound Type and Vaccination History

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client how to use an epinephrine auto-injector for severe allergies. Correct technique includes:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Injecting through clothing is never considered an acceptable technique, even during a true emergency","B":"Injecting into the outer mid-thigh, holding firmly in place for the manufacturer-recommended duration (often several seconds)","C":"Injecting only into the abdomen, rather than the recommended outer mid-thigh injection site","D":"Massaging the injection site afterward is considered contraindicated in every possible case"}}
questions.rationale: Standard epinephrine auto-injector technique involves injecting into the outer mid-thigh (which can be done through clothing if necessary in an emergency) and holding the device firmly in place for the manufacturer-specified duration to ensure full medication delivery before removing it.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Epinephrine Auto-Injector
questions.source_detail: Proper Injection Technique

questions.stem: A client asks the nurse how to properly store their insulin at home. The nurse should explain that unopened insulin vials/pens should generally be:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Refrigerated, while an in-use vial/pen can typically be kept at room temperature for a limited period per the specific product's labeling","B":"Left sitting in direct sunlight in order to help keep the insulin vial at a warmer room temperature","C":"Stored in the freezer, since freezing is thought to extend the insulin's overall shelf life and potency","D":"Stored at any temperature at all, since insulin is thought to require no specific temperature-related storage guidance"}}
questions.rationale: Unopened insulin is generally stored in the refrigerator to maintain potency until the expiration date, while an in-use vial or pen can typically be kept at room temperature for a limited period (varying by specific product, often around 28-42 days) per the manufacturer's labeling. Insulin should never be frozen or exposed to extreme heat/direct sunlight, which can degrade its effectiveness.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Insulin Storage Guidance
questions.source_detail: Proper Insulin Storage Practices

questions.stem: A nurse is administering a chemotherapy medication classified as a vesicant through a peripheral IV, and a colleague mentions this classification just means it's a bit irritating like many other chemo drugs. The nurse understands that if this particular medication extravasates (leaks into surrounding tissue), it can instead cause:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"No significant local tissue damage at all if this particular medication were to extravasate, contrary to its vesicant classification","B":"Severe local tissue damage, including blistering and necrosis, distinguishing a vesicant from a milder \"irritant\"","C":"Systemic effects just, with fairly little meaningful risk of local tissue damage occurring at the actual site of infusion itself","D":"Just mild, temporary skin redness with fairly little lasting local tissue effect from an extravasation event like this one"}}
questions.rationale: Vesicant chemotherapy agents can cause severe local tissue damage, including blistering, tissue necrosis, and potentially permanent injury, if they extravasate into surrounding tissue — a more severe classification than "irritant" agents, which cause discomfort or inflammation but generally not tissue necrosis. Frequent site monitoring during administration is essential.
questions.source_name: Oncology Nursing Society — Vesicant vs. Irritant Classification and Extravasation Management
questions.source_detail: Tissue Damage Risk of Vesicant Extravasation

questions.stem: A client using an albuterol inhaler for asthma reports tremor and a rapid heart rate after use. The nurse should recognize these as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A sign that the inhaled medication is not working and the dose should be doubled","B":"Common, expected adverse effects of the beta-2 agonist, related to systemic beta receptor stimulation","C":"A sign of a severe allergic reaction requiring immediate emergency treatment rather than routine monitoring","D":"Findings entirely unrelated to the client's recent use of the inhaled medication"}}
questions.rationale: Tremor and tachycardia are common, expected adverse effects of albuterol and other beta-2 agonists, resulting from some systemic beta-adrenergic stimulation even though the medication is targeted at the lungs. These effects are generally mild and self-limited but should be reported if severe or persistent.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Albuterol
questions.source_detail: Common Adverse Effects: Tremor and Tachycardia

questions.stem: A provider decides to switch a client from one opioid to another due to inadequate pain control, and a new nurse assumes the new medication should just be started at the same milligram dose as the old one. The nurse understands that "equianalgesic dosing" is actually used to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Ensure the new opioid dose provides comparable pain relief to the previous one, accounting for differences in potency","B":"Automatically doubling the previous opioid dose when switching to the new medication without further calculation of any kind","C":"Eliminating the need for any dose calculation, largely bypassing what equianalgesic dosing actually requires for a switch like this one","D":"Applying this dose conversion process just when switching to a non-opioid medication rather than an opioid-to-opioid switch like the one here"}}
questions.rationale: Equianalgesic dosing uses established conversion ratios to calculate a starting dose of a new opioid that provides comparable pain relief to the previous opioid, accounting for differences in relative potency between different opioid medications, though doses are often reduced initially to account for incomplete cross-tolerance.
questions.source_name: Clinical Pain Management References — Opioid Rotation and Equianalgesic Dosing
questions.source_detail: Purpose of Equianalgesic Dose Conversion

questions.stem: A client who has taken a proton pump inhibitor for an extended period wants to stop it abruptly this week because they feel their reflux has fully resolved. The nurse should explain that stopping abruptly this way may cause:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Rebound acid hypersecretion, with worsening of reflux or ulcer-related symptoms temporarily, contrary to the client's plan to just stop taking it now","B":"No noticeable effect at all on the client's gastric acid production after stopping, supporting the client's plan to discontinue it abruptly","C":"An improvement in overall gastric function with no associated risk of symptom return, supporting the client's plan to stop taking it now","D":"An immediate, permanent cure of the client's underlying gastrointestinal condition, supporting the client's belief that it has now fully resolved"}}
questions.rationale: Abrupt discontinuation of long-term PPI therapy can cause rebound acid hypersecretion, a temporary increase in gastric acid production above baseline, which may worsen reflux or ulcer-related symptoms. A gradual taper is often recommended when discontinuing long-term PPI therapy.
questions.source_name: Clinical Gastroenterology References — PPI Discontinuation and Rebound Acid Hypersecretion
questions.source_detail: Rebound Effect with Abrupt PPI Discontinuation
